solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Maid struggling with a mess — newspapers etc

indicators.note: a word that is struggling is thrashing about, out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder, joined to MAID by 'with'

explanation.surface: A domestic servant battles a chaotic house, with the papers strewn everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash splits the clue: everything before it is wordplay, and 'newspapers etc' after it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The mass media are newspapers, broadcasters and the like, so 'newspapers etc' names them.

clue.text: City two goals up? Not quite

indicators.note: in a down entry, 'up' turns the letters to read bottom to top
not quite the whole thing: the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a goal is an AIM, and there are two of them

explanation.surface: A football fan asks whether the city side is two goals up, and gets a hesitant answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goals' wants to be football scores, but here it means aims. The whole reversal reads MIAMIA, one letter too long, which 'Not quite' trims.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the Florida resort is one example of a city.

clue.text: Periodically squirt yellow liquid around loch or lake

indicators.note: at regular intervals: take every other letter
'around' means surrounding

blocks.note: letters 1, 3 and 5 of SqUiRt
pus is the yellowish fluid of an infection
L is the map abbreviation for loch, placed inside PUS to give PLUS

explanation.surface: A grim little picture of something yellow squirting out near a Scottish loch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loch or lake' reads as one phrase, but the split is after 'loch': 'or' is the link and 'lake' alone is the definition, in the sense of a wine lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialised sense: under European farm policy, a wine or milk lake was a large stockpiled excess of liquid produce.

clue.text: Current article in Berliner Zeitung probing what’s coming up after the weekend

blocks.clueFragment: what’s coming up after the weekend
blocks.note: Monday follows the weekend
der is the German for 'the', an article you would find in a Berlin newspaper; it goes inside MONDAY after MO

explanation.surface: A news report about a piece in a Berlin paper looking into next week's events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, and the German paper supports that; in fact it means a grammatical article, which in German is DER.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adjectives describe what belongs to the present time.

clue.text: Imagine being embarrassed cycling in the morning

blocks.note: red in the face with embarrassment; cycled to DRE
a.m. = before noon

explanation.surface: Picture yourself red-faced on a bike during the morning commute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' paints a bike ride, but it tells you to rotate the letters of RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to picture something in the mind that is not really there.

clue.text: Lacking oxygen and weak, Mike surrenders to Nick

blocks.note: anaemic = pale and feeble
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet; it is taken out
to nick is British slang for to steal, to rob; ROB takes the M's place

explanation.surface: A breathless, feeble man called Mike gives himself up to someone called Nick.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike and Nick look like two men, and 'surrenders to' like a police arrest; in fact Mike is M and 'nick' is the verb for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientific term glossed plainly: the Greek roots mean 'without air', describing organisms or exercise that need no oxygen.

clue.text: Boring piece of macho humour

indicators.note: the answer is a piece of the text that follows

blocks.note: sitting across the words: macHO HUMour

explanation.surface: A verdict on a tired bit of blokeish comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the wordplay agree: macho humour is exactly the sort of thing to be called ho-hum.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: the phrase imitates a bored yawn, so it describes anything dull.

clue.text: That man will ring and say this?

blocks.note: he'll = he will, with the apostrophe dropped
O is round like a ring

explanation.surface: A guess at what a man will say when he telephones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as a phone call, which is why hello fits the scene, but in the wordplay it is the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition points back at the scene: the greeting is the usual first word when a call connects.

clue.text: Separate issue with new lead character

indicators.note: the first letter is replaced by a different one

blocks.note: to give off smoke is to issue it
the G at the front becomes H

explanation.surface: An instruction to split off a comic or magazine issue once it has a new lead character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead character' suggests the hero of a story; here it means the first letter. The clue does not say which new letter, so the definition and crossings pick the H.
explanation.definitionFit: A business idiom: like bees swarming to a new hive, a division is split away from its parent company.

clue.text: Monkey’s scenery changed to concrete resembling rock

indicators.note: one part of the word is swapped for another

blocks.note: the marmoset is a small South American monkey
a stage set is the scenery; the monkey's SET is taken out
concrete = real, actual; it replaces SET

explanation.surface: A zoo report: the monkey's enclosure has been rebuilt in concrete to look like rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monkey's scenery' reads as a zoo enclosure, but the scenery is part of the monkey's name. 'Concrete' looks like building material and is the adjective meaning actual.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word from Latin marmor, marble: it means like marble, and marble is a rock.

clue.text: Cut short card game faced with ace

indicators.note: given a face, a front: A goes in front

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A card player's hand ends early when faced with an ace.
explanation.walkthrough: The ace belongs in the card game of the surface, but in the wordplay it is just the letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most often used of books and texts shortened for a new edition.

clue.text: Fan of Pacino in every part?

blocks.note: the actor Al Pacino
a lover of something is a fan of it

explanation.surface: A question about a devoted admirer of Al Pacino.
explanation.walkthrough: The parts arrive in reverse clue order: AL first, then LOVER. The question mark flags that 'Fan of Pacino' has to be read as AL LOVER.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom, as in 'aching all over': the phrase covers the whole of something.

clue.text: Slacker regularly ignored algebra past papers

indicators.note: every other letter is skipped

blocks.note: identity papers
skip the odd letters of aLgEbRa, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: A lazy student skipped the algebra past papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Past papers' looks like the set phrase for old exams, but it splits: 'past' is a position word meaning beyond, and 'papers' is identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name someone who avoids work.

clue.text: Organised carpool inspired by second traveller

indicators.note: 'organised' means arranged, so the letters of carpool are arranged afresh

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second; it goes around the anagram
anagram fodder, rearranged and placed between M and O

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a car-sharing scheme at the prompting of a second commuter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traveller' fits the car-share scene, but it is the Venetian explorer Marco Polo.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Venetian merchant is history's best-known traveller along the Silk Road to China.

clue.text: Kind of crime found within Old Testament?

blocks.note: a crime committed by someone within the organisation
the Book of Job is inside the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A question about what sort of offence turns up in the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is a pun: Job is a book of the Old Testament, so read literally the phrase is 'inside, Job'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the idiom for a crime committed with help from within the target, and a literal reading of the biblical book's position.

clue.text: Part of shoe reduced by outlet broke

indicators.note: cut short: the last letter goes

blocks.note: INSOLE, the inner sole of a shoe, loses its final E
a vent is an outlet for air or smoke

explanation.surface: A worn-out shoe part has been cut down beside a factory outlet that has gone bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlet' suggests a shop, which suits a business going broke; here it means a vent.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal word for the informal one: both describe being unable to pay one's debts.

clue.text: One leaving cookie jars in disarray for Victoria’s trainees?

indicators.note: going away from: the I is removed
out of order: rearrange the rest

blocks.note: one = I, the Roman numeral; it is taken out
COOKIEJARS without its I, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone walks off leaving the biscuit tins in a mess for Victoria's kitchen staff.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria looks like a woman's name, but it is the Australian state; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional word: in Australian English it names a young trainee on a sheep or cattle station, and Victoria is an Australian state.

clue.text: Faux pas from boss scratching backside

indicators.note: scratching out its back end: the last letter goes

blocks.note: British slang for the boss is a six-letter word ending in R; that R is dropped

explanation.surface: An office embarrassment: the boss caught scratching his bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: The boss is the gaffer, British slang for a foreman or manager. The surface's rude image is the faux pas itself, which is why it hides so well.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: English uses a French word for a social blunder, and this one also came via French.

clue.text: Some peculiar draughts from below barrier

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used
in a down entry, read from the bottom up

blocks.note: sitting across the words: pecuLIAR DRAUGhts, then read backwards

explanation.surface: Strange cold air rising up from beneath a fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draughts' tempts you towards the board game or cold air, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a protective rail along a road or stairway is one kind of barrier.

clue.text: Optimistic divers showing note for doctor

indicators.note: 'showing' means putting on display, so the word now displays the note where it used to show something else

blocks.note: divers is an old word for various, sundry
Dr = doctor; it is taken out
N = note; it replaces DR

explanation.surface: Cheerful scuba divers leave a note for the doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' reads as people who dive, but it is the old adjective meaning several, as in 'divers ways'.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a sunny disposition is bright and cheerful, looking on the good side.

clue.text: North Surrey works where charges are raised

indicators.note: the letters are worked, rearranged

blocks.note: N = north
anagram of SURREY, a county south of London

explanation.surface: A description of an industrial site in northern Surrey where fees go up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like a factory and 'charges' like prices; the definition is about childcare. Surrey is a county just south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic paraphrase: charges are children in someone's care, and raising them means bringing them up.

clue.text: Parrot what’s heard in Dog & Duck

indicators.note: the answer sounds like the words for the two animals

blocks.note: a cocker spaniel is a dog and a teal is a duck

explanation.surface: A parrot copies what it hears in the Dog & Duck, a typical English pub name.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog & Duck is a common English pub name, which makes 'what's heard in' sound like overheard chatter; it is really two animals to say aloud. 'Parrot' could also be a verb, but it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this small crested Australian bird is one member of the parrot family.

clue.text: Comprehensive record yielding times patient discharged by hospital

blocks.note: an index is a record, such as a card index
x is the multiplication sign, times; it is taken out
pt is the medical abbreviation for patient; it takes the X's place
H = hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A detailed medical record lists when a patient was sent home by the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything reads as hospital paperwork, and 'discharged' as leaving the ward; the times are the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe coverage that is thorough rather than superficial.

clue.text: Most arrogant lieutenant charged with failing soldier

indicators.note: going wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: Lt = lieutenant
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A haughty officer is charged over a soldier's failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' suggests a court martial, but it only means loaded with, joining the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A superlative for a superlative: behaving like a lord, above everyone else, is arrogance.

clue.text: Reveal permit to board

blocks.note: as in giving away a secret
allow someone onto a bus or ship

explanation.surface: A pass that lets you board is shown on request.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Permit' looks like a noun, a boarding pass, but it is the verb let.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrasal verb: the idiom for giving a secret away, and the literal allowing someone on.

clue.text: Bit of red in cap worn by lead character in Where’s Wally?

indicators.note: a small part of red: its first letter
'in' places the bit of red within the cap, the way a coloured patch sits in a hat
the first letter of the word

blocks.note: a tip is the cap on the end of something, such as a cue or shoelace
the first letter of red, placed inside TIP
the first letter of Where's, also placed inside TIP

explanation.surface: In the Where's Wally? books, Wally wears a red-and-white bobble hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The book title Where's Wally? has to be broken: 'Where's' supplies W and 'Wally' is the definition, a British word for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for British slang: both are mild insults for a silly, foolish person.

clue.text: Fools originally dole out a lot of money

indicators.note: at the origin: the first letters
most but not all: the last letter goes

blocks.note: first letters of Dole Out
DOSH is British slang for money, without its final H

explanation.surface: Foolish officials once handed out large sums of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of money' reads as a large sum, but it means most of a word for money.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense taken from the extinct bird, thought clumsy and dim, applied to slow-witted people.

clue.text: Letters from disingenuous char

indicators.note: the answer is a run of letters taken from the next word

blocks.note: inside the word: diSINGEnuous

explanation.surface: Insincere correspondence from someone called Char.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Char' looks like a name or a cleaner, or tea, but it is the verb to scorch.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym as verbs: both mean to scorch a surface by burning.

clue.text: One who chooses to push back over dance music

blocks.note: ELECTOR, one who votes, with its O taken out
O = over, from cricket scoring; it moves to the end

explanation.surface: A voter decides to push back against a dance-music track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Push back' suggests resisting, but it tells you to move the O of ELECTOR to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the 1980s synthesizer-and-drum-machine style is one genre of dance music.

clue.text: Panicking, Indiana twice grabs snake

blocks.note: IN is the abbreviation for the US state of Indiana, used twice
the asp is a snake; it goes between the two INs

explanation.surface: Indiana Jones, who hates snakes, panics as he grabs one.
explanation.walkthrough: Indiana Jones famously hates snakes, which makes the scene; in the wordplay Indiana is the state abbreviation IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone in a spin is whirling with agitation, so the phrase works as an adjective for panicking.

clue.text: Attempt to deceive Terry occasionally working

indicators.note: now and then: every other letter

blocks.note: letters 1, 3 and 5 of TeRrY
on = working, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: Someone tries to fool Terry, who is only now and then in work.
explanation.walkthrough: A try-on is British informal for a cheeky attempt to fool someone, as in 'it's a try-on'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British noun: trying it on with someone means seeing what you can get away with.

clue.text: Dead body’s location close to Thames — Hercule Poirot initially puzzled

indicators.note: the end of: the last letter
at the start: the first letter
confused, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the last letter of ThameS
HERCULE and the P that starts Poirot, rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective story: a body turns up by the Thames and Hercule Poirot is baffled at first.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'Dead body's location' read as the start of a crime story, but it is the definition, and Poirot himself is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive paraphrase: this old word for a tomb names the place where a body is laid.
